title: Theory of Modules
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L abstract algebra curriculum: modules over a ring, submodules, homomorphisms, direct sums, free modules, exact sequences, and the structure of finitely generated modules over a PID, building on earlier group/ring theory (MTH300/306).

questions.question: Which of the following best defines a left R-module M over a ring R with identity?
options: An abelian group M with a scalar multiplication R x M -> M satisfying distributivity over both R and M, associativity r(sm)=(rs)m, and 1.m = m
A vector space where scalars must form a field
A group M with a binary operation closed under multiplication by elements of R only
A ring M that contains R as a subring
questions.correct_answer: An abelian group M with a scalar multiplication R x M -> M satisfying distributivity over both R and M, associativity r(sm)=(rs)m, and 1.m = m
questions.explanation: A module generalizes a vector space by allowing the scalars to come from a ring rather than a field, with the module axioms mirroring vector space axioms.

questions.question: Every vector space over a field F is an example of:
options: An F-module
A quotient ring
A free group
An ideal of F
questions.correct_answer: An F-module
questions.explanation: Since a field is a special case of a ring, every vector space over F satisfies the module axioms and is thus an F-module.

questions.question: The set of integers Z, viewed as a module over itself, is an example of:
options: A free Z-module of rank 1
A torsion module
A simple module with no proper submodules
A field
questions.correct_answer: A free Z-module of rank 1
questions.explanation: Z is generated by the single element 1 with no relations, so it is free of rank 1 over itself.

questions.question: Z/nZ, regarded as a Z-module, is best described as:
options: A torsion module in which every element has finite order dividing n
A free Z-module of rank 1
A vector space over Z
An injective Z-module for all n
questions.correct_answer: A torsion module in which every element has finite order dividing n
questions.explanation: For any x in Z/nZ, n.x = 0, so every element is annihilated by a nonzero scalar, making it a torsion module.

questions.question: A non-empty subset N of an R-module M is a submodule if:
options: N is an additive subgroup of M and r.n is in N for all r in R, n in N
N is closed under addition only
N contains the identity of R
N is a subring of R
questions.correct_answer: N is an additive subgroup of M and r.n is in N for all r in R, n in N
questions.explanation: A submodule must be closed under the module's addition (forming a subgroup) and absorb multiplication by arbitrary ring elements.

questions.question: If N is a submodule of M, the quotient module M/N consists of:
options: Cosets m + N with addition and scalar multiplication r(m+N) = rm + N
Only the elements of N
The intersection of M and N
The set of homomorphisms from M to N
questions.correct_answer: Cosets m + N with addition and scalar multiplication r(m+N) = rm + N
questions.explanation: Quotient modules are formed exactly as quotient groups are, with the additional well-defined scalar action inherited from M.

questions.question: A function f: M -> N between R-modules is an R-module homomorphism if:
options: f(m1+m2) = f(m1)+f(m2) and f(rm) = r f(m) for all r in R, m in M
f is bijective
f(rm) = f(r)f(m) treating r and m as ring elements
f preserves only the additive identity
questions.correct_answer: f(m1+m2) = f(m1)+f(m2) and f(rm) = r f(m) for all r in R, m in M
questions.explanation: A module homomorphism must respect both the additive group structure and the scalar action, analogous to a linear map for vector spaces.

questions.question: For a module homomorphism f: M -> N, the kernel of f is:
options: {m in M : f(m) = 0}, a submodule of M
{n in N : f(m) = n for some m}, a submodule of N
The set of fixed points of f
Always the zero module
questions.correct_answer: {m in M : f(m) = 0}, a submodule of M
questions.explanation: As with linear maps, the kernel is the preimage of zero and forms a submodule of the domain.

questions.question: The First Isomorphism Theorem for modules states that if f: M -> N is a homomorphism, then:
options: M / ker(f) is isomorphic to im(f)
M is isomorphic to N
ker(f) is isomorphic to N
im(f) is isomorphic to ker(f)
questions.correct_answer: M / ker(f) is isomorphic to im(f)
questions.explanation: This mirrors the analogous theorem for groups and rings: the quotient by the kernel is isomorphic to the image.

questions.question: A module M is called a free module if:
options: It has a basis, i.e. a linearly independent generating set
Every element has infinite order
It has no proper nonzero submodules
It is finitely generated by one element
questions.correct_answer: It has a basis, i.e. a linearly independent generating set
questions.explanation: A free module is isomorphic to a direct sum of copies of R, i.e. it possesses a basis analogous to vector spaces.

questions.question: Which of the following Z-modules is NOT free?
options: Z/6Z
Z
Z x Z
Z^n for any positive integer n
questions.correct_answer: Z/6Z
questions.explanation: Z/6Z has torsion (every element has finite order), so it cannot have a basis and is not free.

questions.question: A module M is said to be finitely generated if:
options: There exist finitely many elements m1,...,mn in M such that every element of M is an R-linear combination of them
M has only finitely many elements
M has exactly one generator
R itself is finite
questions.correct_answer: There exist finitely many elements m1,...,mn in M such that every element of M is an R-linear combination of them
questions.explanation: This is the direct module analogue of a finitely generated vector space (finite spanning set), though a finitely generated module need not have a basis.

questions.question: A cyclic module is a module that:
options: Is generated by a single element
Has a cyclic group as its underlying additive group only
Contains a submodule isomorphic to itself
Has finite order equal to a prime
questions.correct_answer: Is generated by a single element
questions.explanation: M = Rm for some m in M means every element of M is of the form rm, r in R, so M is cyclic.

questions.question: Every cyclic R-module M = Rm is isomorphic to:
options: R / Ann(m), where Ann(m) = {r in R : rm = 0}
R itself, always
The zero module
A free module of rank 1
questions.correct_answer: R / Ann(m), where Ann(m) = {r in R : rm = 0}
questions.explanation: The map r -> rm from R onto Rm has kernel Ann(m), so by the First Isomorphism Theorem, Rm is isomorphic to R/Ann(m).

questions.question: The annihilator of an element m in an R-module M is:
options: {r in R : rm = 0}, an ideal of R
{m' in M : m' = rm for some r}
The set of all submodules containing m
The zero element of M
questions.correct_answer: {r in R : rm = 0}, an ideal of R
questions.explanation: Ann(m) collects all ring elements that kill m under the scalar action, and it can be shown to be a (left) ideal of R.

questions.question: The direct sum M ⊕ N of two R-modules consists of:
options: Ordered pairs (m,n) with componentwise addition and scalar multiplication
The union of the elements of M and N
Only elements common to both M and N
The set of homomorphisms between M and N
questions.correct_answer: Ordered pairs (m,n) with componentwise addition and scalar multiplication
questions.explanation: The direct sum construction for modules is identical in form to that for abelian groups and vector spaces.

questions.question: An R-module M is a simple module if:
options: M is nonzero and has no submodules other than 0 and M itself
M is generated by exactly one element
M is isomorphic to R
M has trivial annihilator
questions.correct_answer: M is nonzero and has no submodules other than 0 and M itself
questions.explanation: Simple modules are the module analogue of simple groups: they have no nontrivial proper submodules.

questions.question: For a prime p, Z/pZ as a Z-module is:
options: Simple
Free
Not finitely generated
Isomorphic to Z
questions.correct_answer: Simple
questions.explanation: The only subgroups (hence submodules) of Z/pZ are 0 and itself since p is prime, so it is a simple Z-module.

questions.question: A sequence of module homomorphisms ... -> A -f-> B -g-> C -> ... is exact at B if:
options: im(f) = ker(g)
f and g are both injective
im(f) = im(g)
ker(f) = ker(g)
questions.correct_answer: im(f) = ker(g)
questions.explanation: Exactness at a term means the image of the incoming map equals the kernel of the outgoing map.

questions.question: A short exact sequence 0 -> A -> B -> C -> 0 tells us that:
options: A embeds into B and B/A is isomorphic to C
A and C are both isomorphic to B
B is the direct sum of A and C in every case
A is a quotient of C
questions.correct_answer: A embeds into B and B/A is isomorphic to C
questions.explanation: Exactness at A (map from 0) forces injectivity, and exactness at C (map to 0) forces surjectivity, so B/A ≅ C by the First Isomorphism Theorem.

questions.question: A short exact sequence 0 -> A -> B -> C -> 0 is said to split if:
options: B is isomorphic to the direct sum A ⊕ C
A = C
The sequence has infinitely many terms
B is a simple module
questions.correct_answer: B is isomorphic to the direct sum A ⊕ C
questions.explanation: A splitting exact sequence is one where B decomposes as a direct sum of A and a copy of C, equivalently the surjection B -> C has a section.

questions.question: A module M is Noetherian if:
options: Every ascending chain of submodules stabilizes (ACC), equivalently every submodule is finitely generated
Every submodule of M is free
M has finitely many elements
Every descending chain of submodules stabilizes
questions.correct_answer: Every ascending chain of submodules stabilizes (ACC), equivalently every submodule is finitely generated
questions.explanation: The Noetherian condition (ascending chain condition) on submodules is equivalent to every submodule being finitely generated.

questions.question: A module M is Artinian if:
options: Every descending chain of submodules stabilizes (DCC)
Every ascending chain of submodules stabilizes
M has no proper submodules
M is free of finite rank
questions.correct_answer: Every descending chain of submodules stabilizes (DCC)
questions.explanation: The Artinian condition is the dual of Noetherian: every strictly decreasing chain of submodules must terminate.

questions.question: According to the Structure Theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID, such a module is isomorphic to:
options: A direct sum of a free module and finitely many cyclic torsion modules R/(d_i)
Always a free module
A simple module
The zero module
questions.correct_answer: A direct sum of a free module and finitely many cyclic torsion modules R/(d_i)
questions.explanation: Over a PID, every finitely generated module decomposes into a free part plus a torsion part expressed as a direct sum of cyclic modules, generalizing the classification of finite abelian groups.

questions.question: The classification of finite abelian groups (as Z-modules) as products of cyclic groups of prime power order is a special case of:
options: The structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID
The First Isomorphism Theorem
The definition of a free module
Zorn's Lemma
questions.correct_answer: The structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID
questions.explanation: Since Z is a PID, finite abelian groups (finitely generated torsion Z-modules) decompose exactly as the structure theorem predicts.

questions.question: The rank of a free module F over a commutative ring with identity refers to:
options: The cardinality of a basis of F
The number of ideals of the ring
The dimension of R as a module over itself
The order of F as a group
questions.correct_answer: The cardinality of a basis of F
questions.explanation: Rank generalizes dimension from vector spaces to free modules, counting the elements of a basis.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes modules from vector spaces?
options: Modules over a general ring need not have a basis, unlike vector spaces over a field
Modules cannot have submodules
Modules require the scalar set to have multiplicative inverses
Vector spaces cannot be finitely generated
questions.correct_answer: Modules over a general ring need not have a basis, unlike vector spaces over a field
questions.explanation: Because rings need not have multiplicative inverses for every nonzero element, a general module can fail to have a basis, e.g. Z/nZ as a Z-module.

questions.question: The set Hom_R(M, N) of all R-module homomorphisms from M to N naturally forms:
options: An abelian group under pointwise addition (and an R-module when R is commutative)
A field
A subset of M only
A ring with M as its identity
questions.correct_answer: An abelian group under pointwise addition (and an R-module when R is commutative)
questions.explanation: Pointwise addition of homomorphisms is again a homomorphism, giving an abelian group structure; commutativity of R lets one also define a compatible scalar action.

questions.question: In the direct sum decomposition M = N1 ⊕ N2 of an R-module, every element m of M can be written as:
options: m = n1 + n2 uniquely, with n1 in N1 and n2 in N2
m = n1 * n2 for a unique pair
m as an element of N1 only
m as a coset of N1 in N2
questions.correct_answer: m = n1 + n2 uniquely, with n1 in N1 and n2 in N2
questions.explanation: Internal direct sum means every element decomposes uniquely as a sum of components from each summand.

questions.question: A projective module can be characterized as a module that:
options: Is a direct summand of a free module
Has no torsion elements
Is always isomorphic to R
Contains every simple module as a submodule
questions.correct_answer: Is a direct summand of a free module
questions.explanation: Projective modules are precisely those that split off as a direct summand from some (possibly larger) free module, an equivalent characterization to the lifting property.

questions.question: Given the R-module homomorphism f: Z -> Z defined by f(n) = 3n, what is the kernel of f?
options: 3Z
Z
Z/3Z
questions.explanation: f(n) = 3n = 0 only when n = 0 in Z, so the kernel is trivial and f is injective.

questions.question: For the Z-module homomorphism f: Z -> Z/6Z given by f(n) = n mod 6, the image of f is:
options: All of Z/6Z
Only {0}
3Z/6Z
The kernel of f
questions.correct_answer: All of Z/6Z
questions.explanation: Reduction mod 6 is surjective onto Z/6Z since every residue class is hit by some integer n.
